note: The nine collectible voice medallions. Rule, enforced by the renderer: quotation marks appear on screen ONLY when quoteStatus begins with verbatim. Paraphrase cards are styled visibly differently (no quote marks, 'in summary' framing). Portraits only where a credited public-domain image exists in public/media/hyde-park/credits.json; everyone else gets a monogram medallion, never a stand-in photo.

voices.name: Ida B. Wells
voices.role: Journalist and anti-lynching crusader, co-author of the pamphlet handed out at the 1893 fair

paraphrase.text: From the fair's Haiti building, where Frederick Douglass presided, she and Douglass handed visitors The Reason Why the Colored American Is Not in the World's Columbian Exposition, the pamphlet that answered the fair's exclusion point by point.
paraphrase.source: The Reason Why the Colored American Is Not in the World's Columbian Exposition, 1893, public domain

voices.name: Fannie Barrier Williams
voices.role: Educator and clubwoman, the Hyde Park neighbor the Protective Club tried to remove

paraphrase.text: A longtime Hyde Park resident and the first Black woman admitted to the Chicago Woman's Club, she was exactly the settled professional neighbor the 1908 club campaigned against. She refused to leave.
paraphrase.source: National Park Service biography; Chicago Woman's Club records

voices.name: Jesse Binga
voices.role: Banker who wrote mortgages for Black families when almost no one else would

paraphrase.text: His home and his realty office were bombed again and again between 1917 and 1921, more than any other target the commission recorded. He would not move, and he said so publicly.
paraphrase.source: The Negro in Chicago, 1922, bombing case studies; Hayner, Binga, 2019

voices.name: Lorraine Hansberry
voices.role: Playwright; the child in the house behind Hansberry v. Lee

paraphrase.text: She was a child when her family moved into covenanted territory near Washington Park and a mob gathered outside. She grew up to put the memory on stage in A Raisin in the Sun.
paraphrase.source: To Be Young, Gifted and Black, 1969; Hansberry v. Lee, 311 U.S. 32

voices.name: James Baldwin
voices.role: Writer; named what urban renewal was doing

quote.text: urban renewal, which means moving the Negroes out... it means Negro removal, that is what it means
quote.source: Conversation with Kenneth Clark, WGBH, broadcast June 24, 1963, American Archive of Public Broadcasting cpb-aacip 15-0v89g5gf5r

voices.name: Dempsey Travis
voices.role: Realtor and NAACP leader who surveyed the lenders

paraphrase.text: His survey of Cook County's white-run savings and loans found two hundred forty-one institutions and exactly one willing to lend to a Black buyer crossing the line.
paraphrase.source: Satter, Family Properties, 2009, pp. 44 to 45; Travis, An Autobiography of Black Chicago, 1981

voices.name: Clyde Ross
voices.role: Contract buyer in North Lawndale, Contract Buyers League organizer

paraphrase.text: He came north from Mississippi, bought on contract at twenty-seven thousand five hundred dollars for a house the seller had bought at twelve thousand, and spent years organizing so the next family would know the trap.
paraphrase.source: Coates, The Case for Reparations, The Atlantic, 2014

voices.name: Ruth Wells
voices.role: Among the first to stand up in the church basement and say what she had paid

paraphrase.text: When the neighbors compared their contracts, she was among the first to stand and read hers out loud. The league that followed renegotiated contract after contract at fair value.
paraphrase.source: Satter, Family Properties, 2009, Contract Buyers League chapters

voices.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
voices.role: Brought the movement to Chicago's housing in 1966

paraphrase.text: He moved into a West Side flat in 1966 to make Chicago's housing the movement's northern front. The marches he led into all-white neighborhoods that summer pushed open housing onto the national agenda that produced the Fair Housing Act.
paraphrase.source: Chicago Freedom Movement records, 1966; Fair Housing Act, 1968
